questions.stem: The most common cause of diminished coronary blood flow in adults is:
questions.explanation: Atherosclerosis of the coronary arteries is by far the most common cause of impaired coronary perfusion in adults. Embolism, atresia, and fistula are rare.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: Which statement best differentiates ischemia from infarction?
options: Ischemia produces irreversible cell death, whereas infarction is reversible.
Ischemia affects only the pericardium, whereas infarction affects the myocardium.
Ischemia occurs only with valvular disease, whereas infarction occurs only with coronary spasm.
Ischemia is a reversible deficit in oxygen supply, whereas infarction is irreversible myocardial cell death following prolonged severe ischemia.
questions.explanation: This is the core lecture distinction: ischemia is potentially reversible; infarction is permanent cell death. Option A reverses the relationship — a common distractor.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: Which is the earliest functional consequence of myocardial ischemia detectable on echocardiography?
questions.explanation: Abnormal relaxation (diastolic dysfunction) precedes systolic wall motion changes during ischemia. Aneurysm formation requires completed infarction.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: The subendocardium is the myocardial layer most vulnerable to ischemia because it:
options: has the greatest number of capillaries
lies closest to the epicardial coronary arteries
is compressed during systole and is perfused primarily late in diastole under high intracavitary pressure
receives blood directly from the aortic root at very high pressure
questions.explanation: Systolic wall tension compresses the deepest layers, limiting their perfusion; flow to the subendocardium occurs predominantly in late diastole. This makes it the first region deprived and the site of subendocardial (NSTEMI-type) infarction.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: Unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI are collectively classified as:
questions.explanation: Per the lecture breakdown, unstable angina and myocardial infarction (STEMI/NSTEMI) constitute the acute coronary syndromes; stable and variant angina are the chronic forms.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: Coronary blood flow to the left ventricular myocardium occurs primarily during:
questions.explanation: Intramyocardial vessels are compressed during systole, so LV coronary perfusion occurs predominantly in diastole. This is why tachycardia (shortened diastole) worsens ischemia.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: Angina pectoris develops when:
options: the heart rate falls below 50 bpm
myocardial oxygen demand exceeds the oxygen supply delivered through stenotic coronary arteries
left atrial pressure exceeds pulmonary capillary pressure
questions.explanation: Angina reflects a supply–demand mismatch: a fixed atherosclerotic narrowing cannot deliver enough oxygen during increased workload.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: Which of the following lists the diagnostic modalities used for coronary artery disease as presented in the lecture?
options: cardiac MRI and PET scanning only
questions.explanation: The lecture specifies ECG, stress-testing, and angiography for stable angina diagnosis; serum markers are added for unstable angina/MI.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: Which conditions are classified as chronic ischemic heart disease?
questions.explanation: The lecture places stable angina and variant/Prinzmetal's angina under chronic ischemic heart disease; unstable angina and MI fall under acute coronary syndrome. Cardiomyopathies are a separate category.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: Which term describes myocardial dysfunction that persists temporarily after an ischemic episode despite restored perfusion, then gradually recovers?
questions.explanation: Stunning is transient post-ischemic dysfunction after reperfusion. Hibernation is chronic downregulated function in hypoperfused but viable myocardium; both are distinct from necrosis/fibrosis.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: Which of the following is a modifiable risk factor for coronary atherosclerosis?
questions.explanation: Smoking can be modified (cessation is a stated treatment goal in the lecture). Sex, family history, and age are non-modifiable.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: During ischemia, myocardial cells shift to anaerobic metabolism, resulting in:
questions.explanation: Anaerobic metabolism generates far less ATP and accumulates lactate, causing acidosis that impairs contractility. Options A and B contradict the metabolic shift.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: The left main coronary artery normally:
options: bifurcates into the left anterior descending and circumflex arteries
gives rise to the posterior descending artery in 85% of people
courses in the posterior atrioventricular groove
questions.explanation: The left main divides into the LAD and LCx; the posterior descending usually arises from the RCA. Disease of the left main threatens a very large myocardial territory.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: Occlusion of the left anterior descending artery most typically results in infarction of the:
options: anterior wall, apical segments, and anterior septum
questions.explanation: The LAD supplies the anterior wall, apex, and anterior septum. The inferior wall is usually a right coronary territory.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: An inferior wall myocardial infarction with right ventricular involvement most often results from occlusion of the:
questions.explanation: The RCA supplies the inferior wall and frequently the RV via acute marginal branches; proximal RCA occlusion produces this pattern.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: Complete thrombotic occlusion of a coronary artery with sustained transmural ischemia most characteristically produces:
options: transient anginal pain without cell death
questions.explanation: Complete occlusion with sustained transmural ischemia (STEMI physiology) infarcts the full wall thickness. Partial occlusion sparing the subendocardial-sparing outer layers produces NSTEMI patterns.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: A perfusion defect seen during stress imaging that normalizes at rest indicates:
questions.explanation: Reversibility means the myocardium is alive but under-supplied during demand — inducible ischemia. A fixed defect suggests scar/infarction.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: Chronic ischemic heart disease most often leads to which measurable change in LV performance?
options: reduced systolic function with regional wall motion abnormalities
questions.explanation: Repeated or persistent ischemia progressively impairs systolic function with regional hypokinetic/akinetic territories and reduced EF.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: Prolonged complete coronary occlusion without reperfusion ultimately results in:
options: myocyte necrosis with scar formation and permanent loss of contractile function
questions.explanation: This is the lecture's key impact point: infarction is ischemic death of myocardial cells, permanently replaced by non-contractile scar.
tags: Section 1 — Coronary Artery Disease Overview & Ischemia vs Infarction

questions.stem: Which chronic structural complication may develop weeks to months after a large transmural infarction?
questions.explanation: Scarred, thinned myocardium stretches into an aneurysm that bulges and moves paradoxically in systole. The other options are congenital or unrelated. ---
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: The hallmark of stable angina is chest pain that is:
options: provoked by rest and worse with exercise
triggered by exertion or emotional stress and relieved within minutes by rest
questions.explanation: The lecture defines stable angina as exertion-triggered, rest-relieved chest discomfort. Option B inverts the pattern.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: The mechanism of stable angina is best described as:
options: a fixed atherosclerotic stenosis preventing coronary supply from meeting increased demand
spontaneous coronary artery spasm at rest
rupture of a plaque with total thrombotic occlusion
embolic occlusion of a coronary branch
questions.explanation: Stable angina reflects a fixed narrowing; demand rises with activity beyond what the stenotic artery can deliver. Spasm (B) defines variant angina; plaque rupture (C) defines acute coronary syndromes.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: Typical duration of an episode of stable angina:
options: a few minutes, resolving promptly with rest or nitroglycerin
questions.explanation: Stable anginal episodes are brief and predictably relieved by rest or nitrates; pain lasting >20 minutes suggests unstable angina or infarction.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: According to the lecture, diagnosis of stable angina relies on:
questions.explanation: ECG, stress-testing, and angiography are the lecture's stated diagnostic tools for stable angina.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: The drug class emphasized in the lecture for symptomatic relief of stable angina is:
questions.explanation: Nitrates are the lecture's stated drug therapy for stable angina. Anticoagulants belong to unstable angina/ACS management.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: Nitrates relieve anginal pain mainly by:
options: venodilation, which decreases preload and myocardial oxygen demand, plus coronary vasodilation
increasing preload to raise coronary perfusion pressure
blocking calcium channels in the SA node
questions.explanation: Venodilation lowers wall stress and oxygen demand while nitrates also dilate epicardial coronaries, improving supply. Increasing contractility (B) would worsen demand.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: Which lifestyle modification set is recommended for stable angina?
options: smoking cessation, stress reduction, regular exercise, and dietary changes
complete avoidance of all physical activity
questions.explanation: The lecture lists exactly these lifestyle changes for stable angina management.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: Medical procedures used for stable angina refractory to medications include:
options: percutaneous angioplasty and coronary artery bypass grafting
questions.explanation: The lecture lists angioplasty and CABG as the procedures for stable angina. The other options address unrelated conditions.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: In coronary artery bypass grafting, the internal mammary artery or saphenous vein graft is anastomosed:
options: from the aorta to the pulmonary artery
from the coronary sinus to the aorta
from the aorta to the coronary artery distal to the stenosis
from the left ventricle to the coronary sinus
questions.explanation: The graft creates a bypass channel carrying aortic blood to the coronary artery beyond the blockage, restoring distal perfusion.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: The purpose of stress echocardiography in suspected stable angina is to detect:
options: inducible regional wall motion abnormalities appearing with increased demand
questions.explanation: Ischemic myocardium becomes hypokinetic only when stressed; the test reveals supply–demand mismatch not evident at rest.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: During an active ischemic episode, the expected echocardiographic finding is:
options: a transient regional wall motion abnormality in the affected vascular territory
questions.explanation: Ischemia produces transient hypokinesis/akinesis in the territory of the stenosed artery, resolving when perfusion recovers.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: Chest pain that persists more than 20 minutes despite rest and nitroglycerin should raise concern for:
options: variant angina only, with no further workup
questions.explanation: Rest pain lasting >20 minutes is the lecture's red-flag threshold for acute coronary syndrome requiring urgent evaluation.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes stable angina from variant angina?
options: stable angina pain is more severe
variant angina does not respond to nitrates
stable angina occurs with exertion, whereas variant angina occurs at rest, often at night
questions.explanation: Exertion-triggered versus rest/night-triggered pain is the key differentiator. Both respond to nitrates (B is false).
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: Why does rest relieve stable angina?
options: myocardial oxygen demand decreases while the fixed coronary supply remains sufficient for the lower workload
resting raises the heart rate, improving perfusion
questions.explanation: Resting lowers heart rate, contractility, and wall stress, restoring supply–demand balance below the fixed stenotic limit.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: A 58-year-old smoker with hypertension and hyperlipidemia reports chest pressure after walking two blocks that stops when he sits down. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Exertional, rest-relieved chest pressure in a patient with classic risk factors defines stable angina. No rest pain or escalation is described.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: An exercise ECG showing ≥1 mm of horizontal ST depression suggests:
questions.explanation: Horizontal/downsloping ST depression with exercise is the classic ischemic stress-test response, warranting further evaluation.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: Beta-blockers help stable angina primarily by:
options: lowering heart rate and contractility, thereby reducing myocardial oxygen demand
questions.explanation: Slowing the heart rate lengthens diastole (more perfusion time) and reduces demand — the core antianginal mechanism. Beta-blockers do not dilate coronaries.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: Percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty treats ischemia by:
options: dilating the stenotic coronary segment, typically with stent placement
questions.explanation: Balloon inflation and stenting reopen the stenotic segment, restoring antegrade flow through the native artery.
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: In chronic stable angina, the resting echocardiogram between episodes is most likely to show:
questions.explanation: With a fixed stenosis and adequate resting supply, resting wall motion is usually normal; abnormalities appear only during ischemia (or with prior infarction).
tags: Section 2 — Chronic Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable Angina

questions.stem: Which symptom is least characteristic of stable angina?
options: sharp pain lasting several hours at rest
radiation to the left arm or jaw
questions.explanation: Hours of rest pain contradicts stable angina and suggests ACS. Typical angina is brief, exertional, and nitrate-responsive. ---

questions.stem: Variant (Prinzmetal's) angina is caused primarily by:
options: total fixed occlusion of the LAD
questions.explanation: The lecture defines Prinzmetal's/vasospastic angina as chest pain due to coronary artery spasm, not fixed obstruction.

questions.stem: Characteristic timing of Prinzmetal's angina pain:
questions.explanation: Rest occurrence, often nocturnal, is the signature of vasospastic angina and distinguishes it from stable angina.

questions.stem: Which terms are synonyms for variant angina?
questions.explanation: The lecture uses "Prinzmetal's angina" and "vasospastic angina" interchangeably with variant angina.

questions.stem: The ECG during an episode of coronary vasospasm classically shows:
questions.explanation: Spasm causes brief transmural ischemia with ST elevation that resolves when the spasm relaxes — mimicking STEMI transiently but without permanent occlusion.

questions.stem: First-line drug therapy for variant angina is:
questions.explanation: The lecture specifies calcium channel blockers and nitrates for variant angina; both relax vascular smooth muscle and prevent/relieve spasm.

questions.stem: Calcium channel blockers abort coronary vasospasm by:
options: inhibiting calcium influx into vascular smooth muscle, relaxing the coronary artery
questions.explanation: Reduced intracellular calcium prevents contraction of coronary smooth muscle, the direct mechanism against vasospasm.

questions.stem: Which statement about patients with variant angina is true?
options: it occurs exclusively in patients over 70
it may occur with or without fixed atherosclerotic plaques, and is associated with smoking
questions.explanation: Vasospasm can affect angiographically normal arteries or occur at plaque sites; smoking is a major risk factor. It is treated medically, not with routine bypass.

questions.stem: The pain of variant angina is distinguished from unstable angina chiefly by:
options: its episodic, spasm-related pattern versus plaque rupture with thrombosis
questions.explanation: Both cause rest pain, but variant angina is intermittent spasm while unstable angina reflects ruptured plaque and non-occlusive thrombus with impending infarction risk.

questions.stem: An echocardiogram captured during a vasospastic episode may demonstrate:
options: a reversible regional wall motion abnormality matching the spastic artery's territory
questions.explanation: Spasm creates transient ischemia, so the corresponding segments become hypokinetic and recover when the spasm resolves.

questions.stem: If a coronary spasm causes prolonged total occlusion, the potential consequence is:
options: progression to myocardial infarction and life-threatening arrhythmia
questions.explanation: Severe prolonged spasm can completely occlude the artery long enough to cause infarction and ventricular arrhythmias, which is why vasospastic angina must be treated.

questions.stem: Which drug class is least appropriate as sole therapy for variant angina?
options: calcium channel blockers combined with nitrates
questions.explanation: Nonselective beta-blockade leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can worsen coronary spasm. CCBs and nitrates are the correct lecture-listed therapy.

questions.stem: Short-acting nitroglycerin in variant angina acts to:
options: dilate the spastic coronary segment and relieve pain rapidly
questions.explanation: Nitrates are direct vasodilators, so they counteract spasm within minutes. They are not thrombolytic agents.

questions.stem: Historically, provocative agents used to diagnose coronary spasm in the catheterization laboratory include:
questions.explanation: Ergonovine and acetylcholine provoke spasm in susceptible patients, confirming vasospastic angina. Dobutamine provokes demand ischemia, not spasm.

questions.stem: Variant angina should be suspected when:
options: ST depression appears only during exercise
ST elevation appears transiently at rest with pain and resolves when the pain subsides
questions.explanation: Dynamic, pain-linked ST elevation that resolves is the electrocardiographic signature of vasospasm. Fixed Q waves or persistent biomarker elevation indicate infarction.

questions.stem: Coronary spasm most often occurs:
options: at or near a site of endothelial dysfunction or plaque, though the arteries may appear angiographically normal
questions.explanation: Spasm localizes to segments with endothelial injury or atherosclerotic plaque, but may also involve angiographically normal vessels — a hallmark of Prinzmetal's angina.

questions.stem: Which habit is a strong risk factor for coronary vasospasm?
questions.explanation: Smoking injures the endothelium and promotes vasoconstriction, making it a leading trigger for vasospastic angina.

questions.stem: Recurrent episodes of severe vasospasm place the patient at risk for:
options: arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and sudden death
questions.explanation: Prolonged total spasm can precipitate infarction and malignant ventricular arrhythmias, the serious complications of untreated variant angina.

questions.stem: The typical description of variant anginal pain is:
options: a dull ache only when climbing stairs
chest pain that awakens the patient from sleep, not provoked by exertion
questions.explanation: Nocturnal, rest-related pain unprovoked by exertion defines vasospastic angina. Options A and D describe other etiologies.

questions.stem: Cocaine use can precipitate variant angina because it:
options: causes intense coronary vasoconstriction while increasing myocardial oxygen demand
questions.explanation: Cocaine is a sympathomimetic that produces coronary spasm plus tachycardia and hypertension, a dangerous supply–demand mismatch.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old smoker has nocturnal chest pain with transient ST elevation; angiography shows smooth coronaries without significant stenosis. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Rest/night pain with transient ST elevation and angiographically normal arteries is the classic vasospastic angina presentation. ---
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: The clinical significance of unstable angina is that it can be:
options: a sign of impending myocardial infarction
questions.explanation: The lecture's first statement about unstable angina is precisely that it signals an impending MI, demanding urgent treatment.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: Which symptom pattern defines unstable angina?
options: brief exertional pain relieved by rest
pain at rest that is more severe or more frequent, lasting more than 20 minutes
nocturnal pain lasting a few seconds
questions.explanation: The lecture's definition: rest pain, greater severity or frequency, and duration exceeding 20 minutes. Option A describes stable angina.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: In classic unstable angina (versus NSTEMI), serum cardiac biomarkers are:
options: not elevated, because myocyte necrosis has not occurred
questions.explanation: No necrosis means no troponin/CK-MB release; this is the defining biochemical difference between unstable angina and NSTEMI.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: Which medication class is added in unstable angina specifically to limit thrombus propagation?
questions.explanation: Heparin-based anticoagulation prevents growth of the evolving platelet-fibrin thrombus on the ruptured plaque. The lecture lists anticoagulants in its UA treatment set.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: Aspirin benefits the patient with unstable angina by:
options: irreversibly inhibiting platelet aggregation via thromboxane A2 blockade
questions.explanation: Aspirin's antiplatelet effect reduces further thrombus formation on the disrupted plaque; it is not a thrombolytic.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: The underlying pathophysiology of unstable angina is usually:
options: a stable fibrous plaque with no change
plaque rupture or erosion with non-occlusive thrombus formation
coronary embolism from a mural thrombus
questions.explanation: UA sits between stable angina and MI: the plaque disrupts, a partially occluding thrombus forms, and flow is severely reduced but not completely cut off.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: An acute coronary syndrome presentation with rest pain, no ST elevation, and negative troponin is classified as:
questions.explanation: Rest ischemia without ST elevation and without biomarker rise is the textbook definition of unstable angina within the ACS spectrum.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: The key distinction between unstable angina and NSTEMI is:
options: NSTEMI shows biochemical evidence of necrosis with elevated troponin
questions.explanation: Clinically and electrocardiographically they overlap; the troponin rise (myocyte death) is what converts UA into NSTEMI.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: Beta-blockers in unstable angina reduce ischemia by:
options: decreasing heart rate, blood pressure, and contractility
questions.explanation: Lower demand on a supply-limited myocardium is the goal; the lecture includes beta-blockers in UA therapy. They do not cause spasm (and are avoided in vasospastic disease).
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: The appropriate clinical response to suspected unstable angina is:
options: emergency evaluation with continuous ECG monitoring and serum markers
an immediate treadmill stress test at presentation
questions.explanation: Because UA may progress to infarction, patients require emergency assessment, monitoring, biomarkers, and treatment — not outpatient management or stress testing.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: "Crescendo" angina refers to angina that is:
options: new-onset or increasing in severity, frequency, or duration, occurring at lower workloads
completely relieved by a single nitroglycerin tablet
questions.explanation: An escalating pattern defines unstable ("crescendo") angina and reflects a worsening plaque lesion.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: A 64-year-old has had 40 minutes of chest pain at rest. Which finding most strongly indicates myocardial necrosis rather than unstable angina?
questions.explanation: Troponin elevation is the specific marker of myocyte necrosis, separating NSTEMI from unstable angina. ST depression and T inversions occur in both.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: In the acute phase, echocardiography in unstable angina is most useful to:
options: identify regional wall motion abnormalities and assess overall LV function
questions.explanation: Echo detects transient or persistent wall motion abnormalities and quantifies global systolic function; it cannot directly visualize the coronaries (that requires angiography).
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: Nitrates in unstable angina relieve pain by:
options: venodilation to reduce preload and myocardial oxygen demand, plus coronary vasodilation
questions.explanation: The lecture lists nitrates for UA; their supply–demand benefit is the same as in stable angina. Antiplatelet action belongs to aspirin.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: Per the lecture, unstable anginal pain lasting longer than which duration is particularly concerning?
questions.explanation: More than 20 minutes of pain is the lecture's explicit threshold in the unstable angina symptom definition.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: High-risk unstable angina patients are typically managed with:
options: early coronary angiography with revascularization (PCI or CABG)
questions.explanation: High-risk patients undergo early invasive strategy: angiography followed by angioplasty or bypass to treat the culprit lesion.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: Which feature is characteristic of unstable rather than stable angina?
options: new-onset rest pain or an escalating pattern of attacks
questions.explanation: New-onset, rest-related, or worsening angina defines instability. Stable angina is the exertional, rest-relieved, brief pattern.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: Histologically, the culprit lesion in unstable angina typically shows:
options: a ruptured thin-cap plaque with a platelet-rich thrombus
questions.explanation: The "vulnerable" thin-cap plaque ruptures, exposing thrombogenic material and triggering platelet-rich thrombus — the mechanism of ACS.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: Supplemental oxygen is administered in acute coronary syndromes when:
options: oxygen saturation is low, to improve oxygen delivery to the ischemic myocardium
the patient routinely requests it for years
questions.explanation: Oxygen is part of the lecture's UA/MI treatment list and is targeted at hypoxemia to maximize oxygen delivery to ischemic tissue.
tags: Section 4 — Unstable Angina & Acute Coronary Syndromes

questions.stem: Which biomarker pattern supports a diagnosis of unstable angina rather than NSTEMI?
options: CK-MB twice the upper limit of normal
questions.explanation: Persistently negative troponins despite rest ischemia = unstable angina; any biomarker elevation indicates infarction (NSTEMI). ---

questions.stem: Myocardial infarction is defined as:
options: ischemic death of myocardial cells due to complete occlusion of a coronary artery
questions.explanation: This is the lecture's exact definition: ischemic death of myocardial cells from complete coronary occlusion.

questions.stem: STEMI is characterized by:
options: complete coronary occlusion causing transmural ischemia with ST elevation on ECG
questions.explanation: Total occlusion and full-thickness (transmural) ischemia generate the ST-elevation pattern and require emergency reperfusion.

questions.stem: NSTEMI differs from STEMI in that NSTEMI usually involves:
options: total permanent occlusion with transmural necrosis
partial/non-occlusive thrombus causing subendocardial infarction with ST depression or T-wave inversion
questions.explanation: NSTEMI is subendocardial necrosis from incomplete occlusion; the subendocardium is the most ischemia-vulnerable layer. Biomarkers are elevated (B is false).

questions.stem: Which symptom constellation is typical of acute myocardial infarction?
options: burning epigastric pain relieved by antacids
severe chest pain radiating to the arms or neck, with shortness of breath, nausea, and lightheadedness
questions.explanation: The lecture lists these classic MI symptoms: severe radiating chest pain, SOB, nausea, lightheadedness.

questions.stem: Diagnosis of myocardial infarction relies on:
questions.explanation: The lecture lists ECG, serum markers, and angiography as MI diagnostic tools.

questions.stem: Per the lecture, initial treatment of myocardial infarction includes:
options: oxygen, pain relief, aspirin, and nitrates
questions.explanation: The lecture's MI treatment list begins with oxygen, pain relief, aspirin, and nitrates, plus emergency reperfusion in practice.

questions.stem: The ECG hallmark of STEMI is:
options: ST elevation in two or more contiguous leads
questions.explanation: ST elevation in anatomically adjacent leads localizes the transmural injury and defines the STEMI diagnosis.

questions.stem: ST elevation in leads V1–V4 suggests occlusion of the:
questions.explanation: The anterior/septal precordial leads reflect the LAD territory; occlusion there produces an anterior STEMI.

questions.stem: ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF localizes the infarct to the:
questions.explanation: The inferior leads view the diaphragmatic surface, usually supplied by the right coronary artery.

questions.stem: The urgent goal in STEMI management is:
options: rapid reperfusion of the occluded artery — "time is muscle"
questions.explanation: Every minute of total occlusion kills myocardium; primary PCI (or thrombolysis) must occur emergently to salvage tissue.

questions.stem: Serum troponin after myocardial infarction:
options: rises only after 24 hours and stays elevated for life
begins rising within hours of necrosis and remains elevated for days
questions.explanation: Troponin is released as myocytes die: detectable within a few hours, peaking around 24 hours, and remaining elevated for roughly 7–10 days.

questions.stem: A patient with chest pain, ST depression in V4–V6, and a troponin of 2.0 ng/mL is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Ischemic ECG changes plus elevated troponin (necrosis) without ST elevation = NSTEMI.

questions.stem: The expected echocardiographic hallmark after a completed MI is:
options: a regional wall motion abnormality (hypokinesis or akinesis) in the infarct territory
increased E-point septal separation with normal EF
questions.explanation: Dead myocardium is hypokinetic or akinetic in the distribution of the occluded artery — the resting echo signature of infarction.

questions.stem: An ischemic wall motion abnormality involving a papillary muscle may acutely produce:
options: acute mitral regurgitation with a flail leaflet
questions.explanation: Infarction or rupture of a papillary muscle eliminates its chordal support, allowing prolapse/flail and sudden severe MR.

questions.stem: Rupture of the interventricular septum after MI results in:
options: an acquired ventricular septal defect with a left-to-right shunt
questions.explanation: Septal rupture creates a post-infarction VSD; echo shows turbulent left-to-right flow and a step-up in right-heart oxygen saturation.

questions.stem: Free wall rupture 3–7 days after MI most often causes:
questions.explanation: Blood escapes into the pericardial space, causing hemopericardium and tamponade — usually fatal without immediate intervention.

questions.stem: Chronic post-infarction remodeling can lead to:
options: LV aneurysm formation with reduced EF and risk of mural thrombus
questions.explanation: Scarred myocardium stretches into an aneurysm; blood stasis within it promotes mural thrombus and embolic risk.

questions.stem: The long-term functional impact of infarcted myocardium, as opposed to ischemic myocardium, is:
options: permanent loss of contractile tissue replaced by non-functioning scar
questions.explanation: Infarction is irreversible; ischemia is the reversible state. This distinction is a stated lecture objective.

questions.stem: Definitive treatment for acute STEMI is:
options: emergent reperfusion by primary PCI (or thrombolytics when PCI is unavailable)
questions.explanation: Opening the occluded artery immediately is the only therapy that limits infarct size. Adjunctive drugs (oxygen, aspirin, nitrates, pain relief) support but do not replace reperfusion.

questions.stem: On echocardiography, a post-infarct segment that bulges outward and moves paradoxically during systole is described as:
questions.explanation: Dyskinesis (outward paradoxical motion) indicates a thinned aneurysmal segment, more severe than hypokinesis (reduced motion) or akinesis (no motion). ---

questions.stem: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is best described as:
options: an acquired infection of the myocardium
dilation of all four cardiac chambers
an inherited condition causing marked left ventricular hypertrophy
questions.explanation: The lecture defines HCM as inherited (genetic) LV hypertrophy, typically from sarcomere protein mutations passed in an autosomal dominant pattern.

questions.stem: The classic echocardiographic finding in HCM is:
options: global hypokinesis with a dilated cavity
asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a septal-to-posterior-wall ratio greater than 1.3
questions.explanation: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy (ASH) is the HCM hallmark on echo; the disproportionate septum bulges into the outflow tract. Global dilation/hypokinesis defines DCM.

questions.stem: Systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve refers to:
options: anterior displacement of the mitral leaflets toward the septum in systole, causing LV outflow obstruction and mitral regurgitation
questions.explanation: SAM is the dynamic component of obstruction in HCM: systolic flow drags the leaflets into the narrowed LVOT, simultaneously obstructing flow and causing MR.

questions.stem: Classic symptoms of HCM include:
options: shortness of breath, chest pain, and syncope, especially with exertion
questions.explanation: The lecture lists SOB, chest pain, and syncope as HCM symptoms; syncope with exertion in a young patient is a classic red flag.

questions.stem: The diagnostic modalities of choice for HCM are:
questions.explanation: The lecture states echo and ECG diagnose HCM; echo directly demonstrates the hypertrophy, SAM, and dynamic gradient.

questions.stem: The mainstay drug treatment of symptomatic obstructive HCM is:
questions.explanation: The lecture specifies beta-blockers: they slow the heart rate, improve diastolic filling time, and reduce the dynamic outflow gradient. Nitrates/vasodilators/inotropes worsen obstruction.

questions.stem: Dynamic LV outflow obstruction in HCM results from:
options: the hypertrophied septum narrowing the outflow tract, worsened by SAM drawing the leaflets into the flow stream
questions.explanation: Obstruction is dynamic and variable: septal bulge plus SAM interact with flow, so the gradient changes with loading conditions — unlike fixed lesions.

questions.stem: The characteristic continuous-wave Doppler spectral pattern of LVOT obstruction in HCM is:
options: an early-peaking trace identical to fixed aortic stenosis
questions.explanation: Because obstruction worsens in mid-to-late systole as flow accelerates, the CW envelope is late-peaking and dagger-shaped; fixed stenosis produces an early-peaking dome.

questions.stem: The mitral regurgitation jet associated with SAM in HCM is typically:
options: posteriorly directed, opposite the obstructed outflow
questions.explanation: SAM causes malcoaptation with the jet directed posteriorly, away from the LVOT jet; two separate high-velocity signals (LVOT and MR) must be distinguished.

questions.stem: Which conditions or maneuvers increase the LVOT gradient in HCM?
options: dehydration, exercise, and vasodilators (decreased preload and afterload)
questions.explanation: Anything reducing preload or afterload lets the hypertrophied septum appose the mitral leaflets more closely, increasing obstruction; squatting/handgrip and beta-blockers reduce the gradient.

questions.stem: Which medication should generally be avoided in obstructive HCM?
options: digoxin and other positive inotropes or vasodilators
questions.explanation: Inotropes increase contraction (worsening SAM) and vasodilators lower afterload/preload, both increasing the gradient — the opposite of therapy goals.

questions.stem: HCM is distinguished from hypertrophy due to long-standing hypertension or athletic training by:
options: a uniformly concentric pattern in every case
an asymmetric hypertrophy pattern, often with a family history of sudden cardiac death
questions.explanation: Asymmetry, familial occurrence, and sudden-death history point to genetic HCM rather than pressure-overload or athlete's heart.

questions.stem: A feared complication of HCM in young athletes is:
options: infective endocarditis of the tricuspid valve
sudden cardiac death from ventricular arrhythmia
questions.explanation: HCM is the leading cause of sudden death in young athletes, driven by ventricular arrhythmias — hence exercise-related syncope demands prompt evaluation.

questions.stem: When medications fail to relieve obstructive symptoms in HCM, invasive options include:
options: surgical septal myectomy or alcohol septal ablation
heart transplantation as the routine first step
questions.explanation: Myectomy (or alcohol ablation) thins the basal septum and widens the LVOT, reducing the dynamic gradient in drug-refractory obstructive HCM.

questions.stem: Diastolic function in HCM is typically:
options: impaired, from a stiff, thick, noncompliant left ventricle
questions.explanation: Massive hypertrophy stiffens the ventricle, impairing relaxation and filling; this contributes to dyspnea and elevated filling pressures.

questions.stem: LV outflow obstruction in HCM is quantified by:
options: tissue Doppler of the septum only
continuous-wave Doppler across the outflow tract using the simplified Bernoulli equation
questions.explanation: CW Doppler captures the peak LVOT velocity, converted to a peak instantaneous gradient (ΔP = 4v²); this is the standard severity measure.

questions.stem: The apical variant of HCM characteristically shows:
questions.explanation: Apical hypertrophy obliterates the apex, creating the spade-like cavity contour classically paired with giant T-wave inversions on ECG.

questions.stem: Concentric LV hypertrophy in which all walls thicken uniformly is:
options: less typical of HCM, which is classically asymmetric, and more suggestive of hypertensive or infiltrative disease
questions.explanation: HCM is classically asymmetric septal; uniform thickening should prompt consideration of hypertension, aortic stenosis, or infiltrative/storage disease instead.

questions.stem: Until late in the disease, systolic function in HCM is typically:
options: judged by EF alone as the key finding
questions.explanation: The thick-walled, small-cavity LV ejects vigorously (often EF > 70%); the problem is obstruction and filling, not global systolic failure until end-stage.

questions.stem: Performance of the Valsalva maneuver during an HCM echocardiogram:
options: decreases preload, bringing the septum closer to the mitral leaflets and increasing the obstruction
questions.explanation: Strain reduces venous return; a smaller LV intensifies septal–leaflets contact and augments the murmur and Doppler gradient — a classic provocative test. ---

questions.stem: Dilated cardiomyopathy is defined by:
options: progressive dilation of the ventricles with impaired systolic contraction
normal chamber sizes with reduced ejection fraction
questions.explanation: DCM is progressive cardiac dilation with systolic pump failure — the ventricle enlarges and contracts poorly.

questions.stem: Per the lecture, the etiology of DCM is:
options: mostly genetic, but also infections, alcohol, and chemotherapeutic agents
questions.explanation: The lecture lists genetic causes as predominant, with infections (viral myocarditis), alcohol, and chemotherapy (e.g., anthracyclines) as other etiologies.

questions.stem: Typical presenting symptoms of DCM are:
options: heart failure symptoms — shortness of breath and reduced exercise capacity
questions.explanation: Low-output and congestion symptoms (SOB, reduced exercise tolerance) dominate; syncope alone is more typical of HCM or arrhythmia.

questions.stem: Diagnostic evaluation of DCM includes:
questions.explanation: The lecture specifies echo and ECG for DCM diagnosis; echo quantifies dilation, EF, and valve function.

questions.stem: The lecture lists which treatments for DCM?
options: ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, diuretics, digoxin, and alcohol avoidance
calcium channel blockers and nitrates only
questions.explanation: This matches the lecture exactly; these agents improve contractility, unload the ventricle, control congestion, and remove cardiac toxins.

questions.stem: The expected echocardiographic picture in advanced DCM is:
options: a dilated LV with global hypokinesis and reduced ejection fraction
a normal LV with severe aortic stenosis
questions.explanation: Dilation plus global hypokinesis and low EF is the classic DCM echo, distinguishing it from the small, hyperdynamic LV of HCM.

questions.stem: On M-mode echocardiography, DCM commonly shows an increased:
questions.explanation: Poor mitral leaflet excursion in a dilated, poorly contracting LV widens the E-point-to-septum distance; EPSS is a quick bedside marker of low EF.

questions.stem: Mitral and tricuspid regurgitation in DCM are usually:
options: functional, from annular dilation and papillary muscle displacement preventing coaptation
questions.explanation: The structurally normal leaflets fail to coapt because the ventricle and annulus dilate and the papillary muscles are displaced — secondary ("functional") regurgitation.

questions.stem: Which finding would be unexpected in DCM?
options: systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve with dynamic outflow obstruction
questions.explanation: SAM and dynamic obstruction belong to HCM; in DCM the problem is dilation with poor coaptation, not outflow tract obstruction.

questions.stem: Doppler in advanced DCM often shows:
options: a restrictive mitral inflow pattern (tall E wave, short deceleration time) indicating elevated filling pressures
continuous diastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta
questions.explanation: As DCM progresses, filling pressures rise and the E/A pattern becomes restrictive; the dagger shape (C) indicates HCM obstruction, and diastolic aortic reversal (D) indicates severe AR.

questions.stem: According to the lecture conclusions, the only cure for end-stage cardiomyopathy is:
questions.explanation: The lecture's conclusion is explicit: medications manage symptoms, but heart replacement is the only cure for cardiomyopathies.

questions.stem: ACE inhibitors benefit DCM by:
options: reducing afterload and adverse neurohormonal remodeling
blocking calcium channels in smooth muscle only
questions.explanation: Blocking the renin–angiotensin system unloads the failing ventricle and blunts the remodeling that drives progressive dilation.

questions.stem: Digoxin acts in heart failure by:
options: inhibiting the Na-K-ATPase pump, increasing myocardial contractility
questions.explanation: Digoxin is a positive inotrope that improves contraction and rate control in atrial fibrillation; it does not dilate vessels or affect platelets.

questions.stem: Diuretics in DCM relieve symptoms by:
options: reducing volume overload, congestion, and edema
questions.explanation: By removing excess fluid, diuretics decrease pulmonary/venous congestion and ventricular wall stress — symptomatic, though not mortality-improving.

questions.stem: Which chemotherapeutic agent is a classic cause of DCM?
questions.explanation: Anthracyclines cause cumulative, dose-dependent myocyte injury leading to a dilated, poorly contracting ventricle — the lecture's "chemotherapeutic agents" cause.

questions.stem: A key echocardiographic contrast between DCM and HCM is:
options: HCM has a dilated, hypocontractile LV; DCM has a small, hyperdynamic cavity
DCM shows a dilated, globally hypocontractile LV, whereas HCM shows a small or normal cavity with thick walls
questions.explanation: Big-and-weak versus small-and-strong (thick) summarizes the two phenotypes; option A reverses them.

questions.stem: Common ECG abnormalities in DCM include:
options: arrhythmias, conduction delay, and low voltages
persistent ST elevation in contiguous leads
questions.explanation: Chamber enlargement, conduction disturbance (e.g., LBBB), low voltage, and arrhythmias (especially AF and PVCs) characterize DCM.

questions.stem: Because of blood stasis in the poorly contracting LV, patients with DCM are at risk for:
questions.explanation: Low-velocity flow in a dilated ventricle promotes thrombus formation on the endocardium, which can embolize — a rationale for anticoagulation in selected patients.

questions.stem: Alcohol avoidance is part of DCM management because:
options: alcohol is directly toxic to myocardial cells and worsens systolic function
questions.explanation: Ethanol is a direct myocardial toxin and a recognized cause of DCM; continued use accelerates pump failure, so the lecture includes abstinence in treatment.

questions.stem: Beta-blockers improve survival in DCM heart failure when:
options: given at maximal dose immediately during acute decompensation
started at a low dose and titrated slowly during clinical stability
used only together with digoxin in acute pulmonary edema
questions.explanation: Chronic low-dose titration counteracts maladaptive sympathetic activation; abrupt full dosing in decompensated failure worsens the low-output state. ---

questions.stem: Stenosis of a cardiac valve is defined as:
options: narrowing of the valve or orifice that obstructs forward flow
backflow through an incompletely closed valve
questions.explanation: The lecture's definition: stenosis is narrowing that impairs forward (directional) flow; backflow (B) is regurgitation.

questions.stem: Per the lecture, valvular disorders are most common in the:
questions.explanation: The mitral and aortic valves experience the highest pressure loads, making them the most commonly diseased.

questions.stem: The primary hemodynamic consequence of stenosis is:
options: a pressure gradient across the valve, with elevated pressure proximal to the obstruction
decreased pressure in the proximal chamber
questions.explanation: The narrowed orifice forces the pumping chamber to generate higher pressure to push blood through, producing the measurable transvalvular gradient.

questions.stem: Chronic aortic stenosis causes the left ventricle to develop:
options: dilation with low EF from the outset
concentric hypertrophy from chronic pressure (afterload) overload
questions.explanation: Pressure overload triggers parallel sarcomere replication: wall thickening with a normal or small cavity (concentric). Dilation with eccentric hypertrophy follows regurgitant lesions.

questions.stem: Chronic mitral stenosis results in:
options: left atrial enlargement, pulmonary congestion, and risk of atrial fibrillation
immediate RV hypertrophy without LA change
questions.explanation: The pressure backs up into the LA (enlargement, Afib risk), then the lungs; the LV is characteristically underfilled and small.

questions.stem: The mitral valve area in MS can be measured noninvasively by:
options: tissue Doppler of the septum only
questions.explanation: Direct planimetry of the orifice and the pressure half-time method are the standard noninvasive MS area techniques.

questions.stem: The most common cause of aortic stenosis in adults over 65 is:
options: calcific degeneration of a trileaflet valve
questions.explanation: Age-related calcific degeneration dominates in the elderly; rheumatic AS is the classic cause in younger patients in endemic regions.

questions.stem: The most common cause of mitral stenosis worldwide is:
questions.explanation: Rheumatic commissural fusion and leaflet thickening remain the leading cause of MS globally; congenital MS is rare.

questions.stem: The simplified Bernoulli equation (ΔP = 4v²) is applied with continuous-wave Doppler to obtain:
options: peak and mean transvalvular pressure gradients
questions.explanation: The measured jet velocity is converted to instantaneous pressure gradients — the core Doppler severity assessment for all stenotic valves.

questions.stem: The classic symptom triad of aortic stenosis is:
options: exertional syncope, angina, and dyspnea/heart failure
questions.explanation: Syncope, angina, and heart failure are the AS triad; their appearance marks decompensation and mandates valve intervention.

questions.stem: The murmur of mitral stenosis is:
options: a low-pitched diastolic rumble best heard at the apex
a systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border
a high-pitched diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border
questions.explanation: Turbulent LA-to-LV flow across the narrowed orifice during diastole produces the apical diastolic rumble, often with an opening snap.

questions.stem: The murmur of aortic stenosis is:
options: a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex
a holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border
a harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids
a diastolic blow along the left sternal border
questions.explanation: Ejection through the stenotic valve creates a diamond-shaped systolic murmur radiating to the neck; option D describes aortic regurgitation.

questions.stem: A normal mitral valve orifice area is about 4–6 cm²; severe mitral stenosis is generally defined as:
questions.explanation: Severity thresholds are mild <2.5, moderate 1.5–2.5, and severe <1.5 cm²; symptoms typically appear in the severe range.

questions.stem: Severe aortic stenosis is generally defined by a valve area of:
questions.explanation: AVA <1.0 cm² (with high gradients, e.g., mean >40 mmHg) defines severe AS in a normal-flow state.

questions.stem: In chronic aortic stenosis, the LV adapts by:
options: developing concentric hypertrophy to normalize wall stress, with a normal or small cavity
questions.explanation: Sustained afterload excess thickens the walls inward; eventually hypertrophy fails, the ventricle decompensates, and EF falls.

questions.stem: Left atrial enlargement from mitral stenosis predisposes the patient to:
options: atrial fibrillation and atrial thrombus with embolic risk
questions.explanation: A stretched, pressured LA develops electrical instability (Afib) and stasis, so thrombus and stroke risk rise — anticoagulation decisions follow.

questions.stem: Per the lecture, treatment of significant valvular stenosis includes:
options: medical management of symptoms with surgical repair
questions.explanation: The lecture states valvular disorders are treated by symptom management and surgical repair — for stenosis, valvuloplasty, commissurotomy, or valve replacement.

questions.stem: Modalities used to diagnose valvular disorders, per the lecture, are:
options: auscultation, echocardiography, ECG, and chest X-ray
urine analysis and stress testing only
questions.explanation: This list matches the lecture exactly; echocardiography is the definitive tool for confirming and quantifying the lesion.

questions.stem: With a continuous-wave Doppler peak velocity of 5 m/s across the aortic valve, the peak gradient is approximately:
questions.explanation: Applying ΔP = 4v²: 4 × 5² = 4 × 25 = 100 mmHg — severe aortic stenosis physiology.

questions.stem: A congenitally bicuspid aortic valve:
options: predisposes to earlier aortic stenosis or regurgitation, often presenting in middle age
questions.explanation: The abnormal two-leaflet architecture concentrates mechanical stress, accelerating calcific stenosis (or causing AR) decades before a trileaflet valve would fail. ---

questions.stem: Regurgitation of a cardiac valve is defined as:
options: incomplete valve closure creating backflow of blood
questions.explanation: The lecture's definition: regurgitation is backflow through a valve that fails to close completely, impairing directional flow in the opposite way from stenosis.

questions.stem: Chronic aortic regurgitation imposes on the left ventricle:
options: volume overload, producing LV dilation and eccentric hypertrophy
questions.explanation: Diastolic backflow returns to a ventricle already filled from the LA, so the LV must handle excess volume — dilating with eccentric (series-replication) hypertrophy.

questions.stem: Mitral regurgitation produces:
options: a diastolic gradient from LA to LV
systolic backflow into the LA, enlarging the LA and LV
questions.explanation: Each systole ejects part of the stroke volume backward, so the LA (receiving the jet) and the LV (handling the volume-plus-return) both enlarge.

questions.stem: Acute severe mitral regurgitation differs from chronic MR because:
options: the normal-sized LA cannot accommodate the regurgitant volume, causing abrupt pulmonary edema with a normal LV size
the LV is always dilated at onset
questions.explanation: Chronicity allows chamber adaptation; acute MR (e.g., papillary rupture, endocarditis) strikes unadapted chambers, so a small hyperdynamic LV meets a stiff, noncompliant LA and flooding lungs.

questions.stem: The murmur of aortic regurgitation is:
options: a diastolic rumble at the apex only
a high-pitched diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border
questions.explanation: Retrograde diastolic flow from the aorta into the LV produces the blowing, decrescendo diastolic murmur; an apical rumble (Austin Flint) may also be heard in severe AR.

questions.stem: Chronic aortic regurgitation echocardiographic findings include:
options: a small, hyperdynamic LV with a thick septum
a dilated LV with increased stroke volume and vigorous (hyperdynamic) contraction
questions.explanation: Volume overload yields a large, hyperdynamic ventricle with high total stroke volume; EF remains high until decompensation, then falls — a late sign.

questions.stem: Prolapse of the posterior mitral leaflet produces an MR jet directed:
options: posteriorly toward the left atrial wall
questions.explanation: The regurgitant jet points opposite the prolapsing (abnormal) leaflet: posterior leaflet prolapse → anteriorly directed jet (and vice versa).

questions.stem: Which aortic root diseases can cause aortic regurgitation?
options: dissection, annuloaortic ectasia, and Marfan syndrome
questions.explanation: Root dilation or dissection pulls the commissures apart, preventing central leaflet coaptation; the valve leaflets themselves may be normal.

questions.stem: Which echocardiographic measures quantify regurgitant severity?
options: vena contracta width, PISA radius, and regurgitant fraction or volume
questions.explanation: These are the standard quantitative tools; EPSS relates to EF, and the others are unrelated to jet severity.

questions.stem: Infective endocarditis can cause acute severe regurgitation by:
options: perforating or destroying leaflets and impairing coaptation with vegetations
questions.explanation: Vegetations erode, perforate, or prolapse leaflets, abruptly converting a competent valve into a severely leaking one — a surgical emergency.

questions.stem: Ischemic damage or rupture of a papillary muscle most directly causes:
questions.explanation: The papillary muscle anchors the chordae; loss of its support lets the leaflet prolapse into the LA, producing sudden, torrential MR. This is the "ischemic damage" valve etiology named in the lecture.

questions.stem: Per the lecture, treatment of significant regurgitation includes:
options: medical management of symptoms and surgical repair or replacement
questions.explanation: The lecture's valvular treatment applies to both stenosis and regurgitation: control symptoms medically, then repair or replace the valve as needed.

questions.stem: In chronic mitral regurgitation, the left atrium:
options: enlarges and becomes compliant, so pulmonary pressures may remain normal for years
questions.explanation: Gradual LA dilation "absorbs" the regurgitant volume at lower pressure, protecting the lungs; decompensation appears only after years — unlike acute MR.

questions.stem: The tricuspid regurgitation jet velocity is used to estimate:
options: right ventricular systolic pressure (adding estimated RA pressure)
questions.explanation: Applying ΔP = 4v² to the TR jet and adding RA pressure gives RV systolic pressure, a routine echo estimate of pulmonary artery systolic pressure.

questions.stem: Among color Doppler parameters, the most reliable single measure for grading MR severity is:
questions.explanation: The vena contracta (narrowest jet neck) is less load- and gain-dependent than jet area; comprehensive grading integrates it with PISA and regurgitant volume.

questions.stem: Rheumatic valvular disease frequently produces:
options: combined stenosis and regurgitation of the same valve, most often the mitral
purely functional TR with normal leaflets
questions.explanation: Chronic rheumatic inflammation fuses commissures (stenosis) while scarring and shortening leaflets (regurgitation), commonly producing a mixed mitral lesion.

questions.stem: Physical findings of chronic significant aortic regurgitation include:
options: narrow pulse pressure and a soft murmur
widened pulse pressure with bounding (water-hammer) pulses
questions.explanation: Rapid diastolic runoff drops diastolic pressure while systolic pressure rises, creating a wide pulse pressure with collapsing pulses — classic chronic AR.

questions.stem: The ventricular adaptation pattern in regurgitant (volume overload) lesions is:
questions.explanation: Volume overload adds sarcomeres in series, so the chamber dilates while walls thicken relatively less — the reverse of the pressure-overload (stenosis) pattern.

questions.stem: Functional (secondary) mitral regurgitation in DCM results from:
options: LV and annular dilation plus papillary muscle displacement preventing leaflet coaptation
questions.explanation: The leaflets are structurally normal; geometric distortion of the dilated ventricle alone prevents coaptation — distinguishing primary from secondary MR.

questions.stem: The primary modality for diagnosing and quantifying valvular regurgitation is:
questions.explanation: Color, pulsed, and continuous-wave Doppler localize the leak, grade severity, and assess chamber consequences; auscultation raises suspicion, echo confirms. ---

questions.stem: A 55-year-old reports substernal pressure after walking uphill, relieved within 5 minutes by rest. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Exertion-triggered, rest-relieved chest pain is the textbook signature of stable angina; nothing suggests rest pain, necrosis, or ventricular failure.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: A 48-year-old smoker awakens at 3 AM with severe chest pain and transient ST elevation; the pain resolves with nitroglycerin. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Nocturnal rest pain with resolving ST elevation in a smoker is vasospastic angina; STEMI would not resolve, and stable angina is exertional.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: A 62-year-old has recurrent rest chest pain lasting more than 20 minutes, more severe and frequent than before; the ECG shows no ST elevation and serial troponins are negative. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Rest pain >20 minutes with an escalating pattern and negative biomarkers exactly fits the lecture's unstable angina definition.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with crushing chest pain has ST elevation in V1–V4 and a troponin of 5 ng/mL. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Anterior ST elevation plus biomarker rise indicates complete LAD occlusion with transmural infarction, demanding immediate reperfusion.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: A 22-year-old athlete with exertional syncope has an echo showing a 25 mm septum, 10 mm posterior wall, and SAM of the mitral valve. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with dynamic LVOT obstruction
questions.explanation: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy plus SAM plus exertional syncope in a young patient is classic obstructive HCM, the leading cause of sudden death in young athletes.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with long-term heavy alcohol use has cardiomegaly, global hypokinesis, and an EF of 25%. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Alcoholic DCM presents as four-chamber dilation with global systolic failure; regional thick walls with SAM would indicate HCM instead.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: An 82-year-old with exertional syncope has a harsh crescendo-decrescendo murmur, a calcified aortic valve, and a mean gradient of 45 mmHg with an AVA of 0.7 cm². The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Calcified valve, systolic ejection murmur, AVA <1.0 cm², and mean gradient >40 mmHg confirm severe calcific AS.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: A 45-year-old with childhood rheumatic fever has an apical diastolic rumble, LA enlargement, and a mitral area of 1.0 cm² by planimetry. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Rheumatic history, diastolic rumble, and a valve area ≤1.0 cm² (critical) establish severe rheumatic MS.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: Which echo finding best supports significant chronic aortic regurgitation?
options: a small LV with low EF
a dilated, hyperdynamic LV with a diastolic AR jet and increased LVOT stroke volume
questions.explanation: Chronic volume overload produces a big, vigorously contracting LV plus the diastolic jet; low EF in chronic AR is a late, ominous sign.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: Per the lecture conclusions, which condition ultimately requires heart replacement as the only cure?
questions.explanation: The lecture concludes that cardiomyopathies — loss of pumping effectiveness from muscle disease — are curable only by heart replacement.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: On stress echocardiography, a new wall motion abnormality appearing only with stress indicates:
questions.explanation: Stress-induced (reversible) wall motion abnormality marks demand ischemia in living muscle; a scarred segment is abnormal at rest and worsens little with stress.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly classifies the forms of coronary heart disease from the lecture?
options: Chronic ischemic heart disease: stable and variant angina; acute coronary syndrome: unstable angina, STEMI, and NSTEMI
Chronic: unstable angina; acute: stable angina
questions.explanation: This is the lecture's exact breakdown: stable/variant angina are chronic; UA, STEMI, and NSTEMI are the acute coronary syndromes.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: Provided a valvular disorder, its effect on blood flow dynamics is best summarized as:
options: both stenosis and regurgitation always increase forward flow
stenosis obstructs forward flow with a pressure gradient; regurgitation allows backward flow through incomplete closure
regurgitation obstructs flow; stenosis permits backflow
questions.explanation: This matches the lecture objective: stenosis narrows and blocks forward flow; regurgitation leaks backward — both impair directional blood flow.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: Which MI type characteristically shows subendocardial (nontransmural) necrosis with ST depression and elevated troponin?
questions.explanation: Partial occlusion injures the ischemia-vulnerable subendocardium (NSTEMI); complete occlusion produces transmural STEMI with ST elevation.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: Which treatment–disease pairing is correct?
options: variant angina — calcium channel blockers; HCM — beta-blockers
DCM — vasodilators only; mitral stenosis — inotropes
questions.explanation: The lecture's exact pairings: CCBs/nitrates for vasospasm and beta-blockers for HCM. Nitrates and inotropes worsen HCM obstruction, making B and C wrong.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: Nitrates have a therapeutic role in which forms of ischemic heart disease?
options: stable angina, variant angina, unstable angina, and myocardial infarction
questions.explanation: Nitrates appear in the lecture's treatment lists for all ischemic forms; they are avoided in HCM obstruction and are only supportive in DCM heart failure.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: Following acute MI, echocardiography is valuable for:
options: assessing EF, wall motion, and mechanical complications such as MR, VSD, and thrombus
questions.explanation: Echo quantifies ventricular function and screens for complications; it cannot measure biomarkers, recanalize arteries, or substitute for angiography in reperfusion.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: Which finding differentiates NSTEMI from unstable angina?
options: an elevated serum troponin indicating myocyte necrosis
questions.explanation: Biochemical necrosis is the dividing line; ECG changes and symptoms overlap between the two syndromes.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: The lecture's conclusion about treatment of coronary heart disease is that:
options: treatment approaches vary with the form of the disease and its prognosis
questions.explanation: Each form demands a different approach: lifestyle/nitrates for stable angina, CCBs for vasospasm, aggressive antithrombotic and reperfusion therapy for ACS.
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation

questions.stem: Untreated severe aortic stenosis progresses to heart failure through:
options: chronic volume overload causing LV dilation
chronic afterload excess causing hypertrophy, then decompensation
questions.explanation: Stenosis is a pressure-overload lesion: concentric hypertrophy initially compensates, then fails, with dilation, low EF, and heart failure — linking stenosis pathophysiology to outcome. --- *End of question bank — 200 questions. Correct answers: 50 each (A, B, C, D).*
tags: Section 10 — Comprehensive Integration: Lecture Review & Echo Correlation
